column2: The Maya seed, the woman seed and the half-moon joined with 'sva' and 'svarga-kha'; '-palaya,' 'sarvadharaya,' 'sarva' and 'sarvodbhava' likewise,
and 'sarvashuddhimaya,' in the dative, near 'sarvasura'; 'rudhira,' 'rati' with long vowel, 'vayu,' 'shubhra-anila,' 'sura,'
'bhajanaya,' 'bhagi,' 'satya,' 'vikapalaya' and the heart syllable — this is the fourth mantra, of six syllables, for worshipping the great conch.
Having worshipped the circle of the nine suns, one should fill the conch with water using the root mantra, regarding it as nectar, with perfume, flowers, unbroken rice and the like.
Showing the three-part mudra, one should worship the circle of the moon; [the mantra is] speech, truth, the lotus and sky, with ra, the grace syllable and the dot.
The root mantra with the calamity-destroying mantra and the visarga — with this the practitioner, restrained, should consecrate the water eight times.
Casting Madisha with Maya, one should show the sky and yoni mudras; meditating there on the circle, the eight petals and the hexagon, one should contemplate the Goddess.
One should worship her as described before and then offer libations with the root mantra, to Maheshvari, using the index, middle, ring and little fingers
together with the thumb, four times, in the water of the great conch; with 'kham' and 'ra' rich in the dot, and with Bhrigu joined to the dot,
beginning with Om and ending with 'namah,' one should offer libations to Ananda-Bhairava. Then with half of that water one should sprinkle the materials of worship.
Showing the yoni mudra, one should bow to the Goddess who carries one across existence. This procedure of the arghya has been declared, granting all success.
On the pedestal described before, on a lotus with a hexagonal pericarp, enclosed by a lovely earth-square, one should worship the Goddess with fine offerings.
In the earth-square, in the four directions, one should worship Ganesha and the others. [Ganesha,] holding in his hands noose, goad, skull and trident,
adorned with ornaments, should be worshipped in the east. [Batuka,] holding skull and trident in his hands, adorned with serpents,
lovely, surrounded by his own troop, one should worship in the south. Holding sword, trident, skull and damaru in his hands,
the dark, naked, fierce Kshetrapala in the west. And the Yoginis, holding skull, damaru, noose and linga in their hands,
young maidens in red clothes, one should worship in the north. On the head one should worship Akshobhya, the auspicious seer of the Goddess's mantra.
[The mantra for] Akshobhya: 'Accept this cloth and flower,' ending with the beloved of Fire; this is the mantra for worshipping Akshobhya, on the hexagon.
One should worship Vairochana, Amitabha, the one called Padmanabha, Shankha and the one called Pandura on the petals in the main directions,
and Labhaka, Manaka, Pandura and Taraka on the lotus petals in the intermediate directions, for success in one's wishes.
Their names, beginning with the dot and the first letter, ending in the vocative, with 'accept this vajra-flower,' ending with the beloved of Fire and beginning with the pranava —
these are declared to be the mantras for worshipping Vairochana and the others. At the four gates, Bhudhara, Padmantaka and Yamantaka,
the one called Vidyantaka and then Narantaka — these one should worship; then Shakra and the others, and the thunderbolt and other weapons, one should worship next.
Worshipping the Goddess thus, one gains learning, wondrous wealth, sons and grandsons, auspicious fame and power over people.
Tara, Maya, 'Shrimadaka-jate Nilasarasvati,' 'mahograTare,' ... with the eye syllable and a pair of 'gadi' —
'sarvadeva-pishacha,' ... 'jadyam cha chhedaya' twice, and Rama —
ending with Maya, the weapon syllable and the beloved of Fire — this is the fifty-two-syllable mantra. With it, while worshipping daily, one should offer an oblation to the Goddess every day.
When the mantra has thus been perfected, the practitioner performs its applications. For a newborn child, within three days of birth,
one should write the mantra on the tongue with honey and ghee, using a golden stylus, or with a white durva grass.
When the eighth year has passed, even that child becomes a wondrous poet, invincible to others and honoured with wealth by hosts of kings.
During an eclipse, making a peg of human bone, lotus and wood in water, one should write with it, using oil, honey and nectar;
write the mantra on a lotus leaf and encircle it with the letters of the alphabet; burying that leaf in a square fire-pit with a girdle,
and establishing fire there, one should offer with this mantra a thousand red lotuses soaked in cow's milk and water.
At the end of the oblation one should offer a bali of various gems and fruits, duly, with the bali mantra; the bali mantra is now revealed:
Tara, 'padme' twice, Tandri, the sky with long vowel, and red; Atri mounted on Visha and Bhaga, saying the word 'Padmavati,'
'Jhinti' with Isha, with Anila and 'svaha' — this is the sixteen-syllable mantra of the offering. Then at midnight one should offer the bali with the mantra described before.
When this is done, he becomes a victor among the learned and a king of poets, the abode of Bharati and Lakshmi, able to delight the people.
The practitioner who wears on his forehead gorochana consecrated with a hundred recitations — whomever he looks upon becomes at once like his servant.
Taking a coal from a cremation ground on a Tuesday in the east, wrapping it with that mantra and binding it with red threads,
consecrating it a hundred times with the root mantra, one should cast it into an enemy's house; within seven days it drives out the opponents with their families.
Writing the night mantra with milk on a human bone, one should consecrate it a thousand times on a Sunday at midnight;
cast into an enemy's house it makes him fall from his realm; cast into a field it destroys the crops...

Inside a hexagon one should write the root mantra and the name of the target, the vowels on the filaments, and outside a petal-circle with the eight groups of letters, surrounded by a lotus and an earth-square.
One should write this yantra on birch bark with jahu juice, wrap it in pure cloth and tie it with silk thread; worn around a child's neck it surely
removes fear of evil spirits; on the left arm of women it gives sons; on the right arm of men it gives wealth to the poor,
knowledge to those who seek knowledge, and victory to kings.
The Kama, Vak and final seed-syllables bring the three worlds under control; one should, restrained, recite the Kama, final and Vani seed-syllables for liberation.
At the beginning of Bala's worship one should worship the three kinds of teachers: the divine stream, the stream of Siddhas and the human stream — thus threefold.
Paraprakasha, Parameshana, Parashiva, Kameshvara, then Moksha, the sixth Kama, and Amrita last —
these seven are the divine stream, each followed by the word 'Ananda.' Ishana, Tatpurusha, the one called Aghora, Vamadeva
and Sadyojata — these five are remembered as the stream of Siddhas, O sage. The human stream is to be known through the tradition of one's own teacher.
In a yantra formed of nine triangles, the best practitioner should write the seed-syllables three times, clockwise, starting from the central triangle.
He should write three syllables each of the Gayatri on the eight petals, encircle it outside with the alphabet, and outside that two earth-squares,
intersecting one another with corners shining with the Kama seed. On a leaf this is called the Traipura yantra, perfected by japa and invocation.
Worn on the arm it gives wealth, fame, happiness and sons. After Kama: 'Tripura devi vidmahe, kamesvari dhimahi,'
'tan nah klinne prachodayat' — so this is declared,
the Traipura Gayatri, granting all success and served by the gods. Now another incarnation of Lakshmi is described, granting success to men.
The Veda's first (Om), Girija (Hrim), Padma (Shrim), Manmatha (Klim), the heart syllable (namah), Bhrigu, 'bhagavati maheshvari annapurne' in the dative, and the wife of Fire (svaha) —
this is declared the twenty-syllable vidya; its seer is Druhina, its metre Dhriti, and its deity is proclaimed to be Annapurneshi.
The six-limbed placement is made with the Hrillekha seed joined with the six long vowels. One should place it at nine places — mouth, nose, eyes, ears, shoulders and anus.
There are nine words; their numbers of syllables are now stated: one, one, one, two, four, four, four, two, one —
measured by the syllables according to the words. Then one should meditate on the queen of the gods, golden-limbed, three-eyed, beautiful with clothes and ornaments,
the Goddess joined with Bhu and Rama, holding in her lotus hands a golden vessel. Japa is one lakh and oblation ten thousand, with charu smeared with ghee.
Worship is prescribed on a pedestal furnished with the nine Shaktis beginning with Jaya, in a yantra with a triangle, four petals, eight petals and sixteen petals,
joined with an earth-square; one should place the mantra with Maya. In the three corners beginning with the south-east, Shiva, Varaha and Madhava
should be worshipped with their own mantras, which are now stated. The pranava, the sky with Manu and the moon, the heart syllable, Shiva
and the wind — this seven-syllable mantra of Shiva is for Shiva's worship. One should first recite the mantras of Varaha and Narayana.
Then, having worshipped the six limbs, one should worship Dhara on the left and Rama on the right with their own mantras, which are stated, O lord of sages:
saying 'annam mahyannam me dehi annadhipataye,' 'mamemam annam pradapaya,' ending with the beautiful one of Fire —
a twenty-two-syllable mantra; for the earth's favour it is enclosed with the earth seed, for Lakshmi's favour with the Shri seed, O brahmin; the earth seed is Smriti with 'la,' Manu and the moon.
This is declared the seed of the earth, and the Shri seed was stated before. One should worship those preceded by the four seeds at the beginning of the mantra:
the four Shaktis in the square — Para and Bhuvaneshvari, Kamala and Subhaga — and Brahmi and the others on the eight petals;
and on the sixteen petals: Manada, Tushti, Pushti, Priti, Rati, Hri, Shri, Svadha, Svaha as the tenth,
Jyotsna, Haimavati, Chhaya, Purnima, Samhati and Amavasya are to be worshipped, preceded by Prana, in the lord of mantras.
In the earth-square are the guardians of the world, and their weapons before them. When this mantra has been perfected by japa and the rest, through heaps of wealth
the practitioner becomes like Kubera, honoured by people. Now another incarnation of Lakshmi is described, best of sages.
The pranava, Shanti, Aruna joined with Kriya and adorned with the moon; 'Bagalamukhi sarva-' at the end, joined with Indhika and Hladini,
yellow, with Jara and Pratishtha, again with long vowel and 'd'; 'vacham mukham padam stambhaya,' then say the word 'jihvam,'
'kilaya,' 'buddhim vinashaya,' ending with her own seed; Tara and the beautiful one of Fire — this is declared the mantra of Bagala.
Its seer is Narada, its metre Brihati, and its deity Bagalamukhi; with syllables numbering two, five, five, nine, five and ten,
one should form the limbs and then meditate on her clad in yellow, seated on a golden throne, golden in colour, the paralyser, crowned with the moon,
holding in her hands a hammer, a noose, a thunderbolt and a tongue. Meditating thus, one should recite a lakh times and offer ten thousand oblations with champaka
flowers; one should worship her on Bala's pedestal. For worship one should draw the yantra with sandal, aloe-wood, camphor and the like,
and worship her in the triangle, six petals, eight-cornered figure and sixteen petals: Mangala, Stambhini, Jrimbhini, Mohini,
Vashya, Chala, Balaka, Bhudhara, the one called Kalmasha, Dhatri, Kalana, Kalakarshini, Bhramika,
Mandaga, Bhogastha and Bhavika, the sixteenth. In the four directions of the earth-square, beginning with the east, one should worship in order
Ganesha, Batuka, the Yoginis and Kshetrapala, and outside them Indra and the others with their weapons.
When the mantra is thus perfected, the practitioner can paralyse even gods and others. Seated on yellow cloth, wearing yellow garlands and unguents,
one should worship the Goddess with yellow flowers and recite with a rosary of turmeric; meditating on the yellow Goddess, standing in water, one should recite ten thousand times.
An oblation of sesame with the three sweets is held to bring men under control; with salt smeared with the three sweets there is surely attraction.
An oblation of neem leaves smeared with oil causes enmity; with tala, salt and turmeric there is paralysis of enemies.
Offering house-soot, mustard, buffalo ghee and guggulu at night in a cremation-ground fire, one quickly destroys enemies.
Offering the feathers of vultures and crows, pungent oil, vibhitaka and house-soot in a pyre-fire, one drives away enemies.
One who offers durva, guduchi and parched rice with the three sweets quells all diseases even by his sight.
On a mountain top, in a great forest, at the confluence of rivers or in a Shiva temple, devoted to celibacy, one should recite a lakh times for every success.
Milk of a cow of one colour, with sugar and honey, consecrated three hundred times and drunk, destroys the effects of poison.
On lovely sandals made of white palasha wood, dyed with lac, one should recite this mantra a lakh times;
a man mounted on them travels a hundred yojanas in a moment. Mercury, red arsenic and orpiment ground with honey,
consecrated a lakh times with the mantra and smeared over the whole body, make a man invisible to others — behold this wonder!
One should draw a hexagon with the seed-syllable and the name of the target, using orpiment and turmeric powder mixed with datura juice,
with the remaining syllables around it, shining in the earth-square; that yantra, with life infused, should be wrapped with yellow thread.
Taking clay from a potter's spinning wheel, one should make a lovely bull and place the yantra inside it;
smearing the bull with orpiment, one should worship it daily; it paralyses the speech, movement and undertakings of enemies.
Taking with the left hand a skull-bowl lying in the cremation ground, one should draw the yantra in it with a coal from a pyre;
consecrated and buried in the ground, it paralyses the movement of enemies. Again, one should draw the yantra with a coal on a cloth from a corpse,
place it in a frog's mouth wrapped in yellow thread and worship it with yellow flowers; it paralyses the speech of enemies.
On the ground where an ordeal is to take place, one should draw the yantra; wiped with the enemies' vessels, it paralyses the ordeal.
The root of indravaruni, consecrated seven times with the mantra and cast into water, paralyses the water in a water-ordeal.
What need of more words? When the mantra is properly worshipped by the practitioner, it paralyses the movement, understanding and the like of enemies; there is no doubt.

[One should place] Dravini, beginning with 'dram,' on the head; Kshobhini, beginning with 'dram,' on the feet; Vashikarani with 'klim' on the face; on the private parts the one preceded by the seed 'blum';
Akarshani on the heart, again the one placed with Bhrigu at the end of all; Sammohini in order — this is declared the placement of the arrows.
On the forehead, between the brows, the mouth, the uvula, throat and heart, the navel and the adhishthana, the five beginning with Tara, Subhaga and the rest [are placed].
From the head down to the navel the practitioner places Subhaga, Bhaga, Bhagasarpini, Para and then Bhagamalini,
Ananga, Anangakusuma, again Anangamekhala, Anangamadana and Madavibhramamanthara —
the chief deities, adorned with colours, ornaments and the like, holding in their lotus hands a rosary, a book, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-giving.
With Vak, Kama, 'blum' and 'strim' at the end of 'sa,' five Taras are declared. Then one should perform the placement called the ornament-placement in the manner described, O sage.
Having placed these on his body, he should meditate on Tripura-Bhairavi, radiant as a thousand suns, clad in red silk,
with a garland of heads, her breasts smeared with blood, holding in her hands a rosary, knowledge, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-giving, with three eyes in her face.
Having received initiation, the self-controlled one should recite the mantra as many lakhs as there are principles, and offer a thousand oblations of flowers from the brahma tree (palasha),
or of oleander flowers smeared with the three sweets. [Her pedestal is] a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp of nine triangles,
joined with the Shaktis beginning with Iccha; one should worship Bhairavi's pedestal. Iccha, Jnana, Kriya, then Kamini, Kamadayini,
Ratipriya, Madananda, and the ninth, Manonmani — these nine Shaktis are declared, holding the gestures of boon-giving and fearlessness.
Vagbhava, the red one 'rayai,' Shrikantha, red Anala, with the long vowel 'yai,' 'para,' then 'aparayai,' joined with 'hasau,'
'sadashiva-mahapreta' in the dative, 'padmasanam namah' — with this mantra one should offer the seat, following the sequence of the revered teachers.
In the space between the east and the middle triangle one should worship, then form the image with five pranavas and invoke the deity into it,
worshipping with concentration according to the procedure of the Agamas. Tara, Vak, Shakti, Kamala, 'hasakhphrem' and 'hasauh' are remembered.
In the left corner one should worship the Goddess's Rati, radiant as the moon, holding goad and noose, gentle, overcome with the delight of passion;
Priti in the right corner, like molten gold, holding a goad and bowed with her two arms, should be worshipped;
in front Manobhava, red, adorned with red flowers and the like, holding a sugarcane bow and flower arrows, with a smiling face.
Then the knower of the procedure should worship the limbs as before, and in the directions and in front, with their own mantras, the deities of the arrows,
holding flower arrows in their lotus hands, radiant with the nectar of salutation. In the eight triangles one should worship the eight Shaktis beginning with Subhaga.
The Mothers, sitting on the laps of the Bhairavas, overcome with the delight of passion, are to be worshipped on the eight petals duly with flowers and the like.
Then the world-guardians in the directions, and their weapons outside them. Knowing this supreme deity through merit earned in former births,
whoever worships her in the way described becomes an abode of riches. When the mantra is thus perfected, the practitioner should accomplish his own aim.
He should offer a lakh, or half that, of flawless red lotuses soaked in the sweets, and daily feed brahmins;
he should please lovely young women, regarding them as the deity; at the end of the oblations he should satisfy his teacher with wealth, grain and the like.
When this is done, the world is under his control and he becomes an abode of Rama. With red lotuses smeared with the three sweets, or red oleander flowers,
flowers and milk-food with ghee, by oblation one brings the universe under control; offering palasha flowers, the practitioner gains perfection of speech.
The wise should offer guggulu with camphor and aloe-wood; by that alone he gains divine knowledge and becomes a poet.
An oblation of pieces of guduchi smeared with milk conquers all untimely death; an oblation of durva smeared with milk for three days gives long life.
With oblations of girikarni flowers one subdues brahmins, with kahlara flowers kings, and with karnikara flowers their wives;
offering jasmine (mallika) flowers one subdues princes, with korantaka flowers vaishyas, and with patala flowers shudras.
Reciting the mantra in forward and reverse order with the name of the target placed within, the practitioner should offer [items] soaked in sweets;
with mustard seeds mixed with honey he subdues kings in a moment, and by the same procedure their wives and sons.
With jati and bilva flowers joined with the three sweets, by oblation one subdues men, women and kings in turn.
Offering malati and bakula flowers mixed with sandal, the practitioner gains poetic skill within a year.
Offering bilva fruits joined with the three sweets, one subdues the world and obtains the prosperity one desires.
One should offer food with ghee and become rich in food; the self-controlled one should offer camphor with musk and saffron,
and at once gains beauty greater than Kandarpa's. The practitioner should offer parched rice soaked in curd, milk and honey,
and conquering all diseases he lives a hundred years. Two parts of sandal, one part of saffron,
one part of gorochana — grinding these three in cool water, one should make a tilaka on the forehead; those he looks upon or who look upon him,
those he touches or who touch him, soon come under his control. One should take camphor, kapi and chora in equal parts,
four parts of jatamamsi, the same of gorochana, saffron in equal part, and ten parts of sandal,
aloe-wood nine parts — in this order of parts; all this, ground well by a maiden in cool water,
taken as a tilaka on the forehead, brings under control kings and men, women full of pride and arrogance, elephants in rut,
lions, tigers, great serpents, ghosts, vetalas and rakshasas — the man wearing the tilaka subdues them by mere sight.
Thus Bhairavi has been described; hear of another incarnation. Vak, Maya, Kamala, Tara, then 'namo bhagavati,'
one should say 'Shrimatangeshvari sarvajana-manohari,' 'sarvamukha-ranjani' after 'sarva-sukha-rajya,'
then 'sarvaraja-vasham-kari,' then the word 'sarva,' 'stripurusha-vasham-kari,' with Srishti, Vidya and Krodhini,
'sarva-dushta-mriga-vasham-kari,' then the word 'sarva,' 'sarvasattva-vasham-kari,' then 'sarvaloka,'
then 'amukam me vasham anaya,' ending with the beautiful one of Fire — the mantra of eighty-eight syllables; its seer and the rest are as for Bhairavi.
The practitioner should perform on his body the placements about to be described in order: on the head, forehead, between the brows, palate, throat, neck and chest,
at the anahata, on the two arms, the belly, the navel, the svadhishthana, the private parts, and the right and left feet,
and at the muladhara and anus, one should place the eighteen words in order, with syllable-counts of three, one, two, four, six, eight, five, nine, eight,
nine, ten, eight, four, three, one, two, three and two — this arrangement is declared, with the letters of the mantra in order.
The wise one should place Rati and the others at the root, heart and between the brows, beginning with the seeds of Vak, Shakti and Lakshmi and ending with 'Matangi.'
One should place them duly on the head, face, heart, private parts and feet; Hrillekha, Gagana, Rakta, and again Karalika,
Mahochchhushma, preceded by the seed formed from the first letter of their names and ending with 'Matangi' — then the practitioner should perform the six limbs.
With twenty-four syllables the heart, with thirteen the head, the topknot with eighteen, the armour with as many syllables,
the eye with thirteen, and the weapon is declared with two. Then one should perform the arrow-placement in the way described for Bhairavi.
At Matangi's feet and elsewhere, the Manmathas on the face and shoulders, the sides, hips, navel region, and again the hip-sides and shoulders,
preceded by the three seeds, the practitioner [places] Manmatha, Makaradhvaja, Madana, Pushpadhanva, the fifth Kusumayudha,
the sixth named Kandarpa, Manobhava and Ratipriya, ending with 'Matangi' — the knower of mantras should place them at these places.
Kusuma, Mekhala, Madana, Madanatura, Madanavega, Sambhava, Bhuvanapala and Indurekhika —
preceded by the word 'Ananga' and ending with 'Matangi' — are to be placed next at the root, the adhishthana, the manipura,
the heart, throat, mouth, between the brows and on the head by the practitioner. First Lakshmi and Sarasvati, Rati, Priti, Krittika,
Shanti, Pushti and again Tushti, crowned with the word 'Matanga'; the knower of mantras should place the root mantra separately on his own head,
at the adhara, the adhishthana, the navel, then the anahata, the throat, between the brows, the bindu, again the kala,
the nirodhika, the half-moon, the nada, the nadanta, the raised shoulders, the mouth, the dhruva-mandala and the Shiva place —
ending with 'Matangi,' one should place Vama, then Jyeshtha, Raudri, Prashanta, the one called Shraddha, then Maheshvari,
Kriyashakti, Sulakshmi, Srishti, Sanjna, Mohini, Pramatha, Ashvasini, Vidyullata and Chichchhakti,
then Sundari, Ninda and Nandabuddhi in order — these, with the three seeds in addition, on the head, forehead, heart and base,
the best teacher should place duly, beginning with 'Matangi'; Matangi herself, preceded by 'Mahat,' and preceded by the word 'Mahalakshmi,'
preceded by 'Siddhalakshmi,' at the root and the circle of the base; and with that the best teacher should perform the pervading placement.
Having thus placed these on his body, he should contemplate the deity of the mantra: dark, listening to the words of a parrot, one foot resting, her hair [loose],
wearing a crescent moon, playing the vina, intoxicated with wine, clad in red, her topknot beautified with a garland of kahlara lotuses,
Matangi with conch-shell earrings, her forehead shining with a painted mark. One should recite the mantra ten thousand times, and a tenth of that with madhuka
flowers joined with the three sweets one should offer for the perfection of the mantra. One should draw a lotus with a triangular pericarp and eight petals,
surrounded outside by eight petals and enclosed by sixteen petals, made square outside, delightful to the eye in its beauty.
On this pedestal one should worship in order these nine Shaktis, beginning with Vibhuti as described before, ending with the word 'Matangi,'
and at the end of all, 'shakti-kamalasanaya namah' — the mantra beginning with the seeds of Vak, Satya and Lakshmi is declared for worshipping the pedestal.
Forming the image with the root mantra and invoking the deity into it, the knower of mantras should worship according to the procedure about to be told.
The wise one should worship Rati and the others in the three corners as before; the five Hrillekhas should be worshipped by the practitioner in the middle and in the directions,
holding noose, goad, fearlessness and boon, radiant as beings; then the knower of the procedure should worship the limbs as before.
One should worship the arrows in the directions and the fifth in front; then in the middle of the petals Anangakusuma and the others are to be worshipped,
red-bodied, holding noose, goad, fearlessness and boon. Again at the petal tips Lakshmi and the others, holding vinas, are to be worshipped.
On the outer eight petals Manmatha and the others, intoxicated with passion, are to be worshipped, and the other limbs beginning with Nishanga, holding flower arrows, quivers and bows.
On the petals the Mothers beginning with Brahmi, of the marks described, are to be worshipped; and at their tips the learned should worship the Bhairavas beginning with Asitanga.
Again on the sixteen petals the sixteen Shaktis beginning with Vama are to be worshipped, dark-bodied, singing with sweet vinas.
In the square, in the four directions, one should worship four more, beginning with Matangi, intoxicated, their hands gleaming with vinas.
In the south-east one should worship Vighnesha, in the south-west Durga, in the north-west the Batukas, and in the north-east Kshetrapa.
The world-guardians are to be worshipped outside with their thunderbolts and other weapons. When this mantra is established, the practitioner should accomplish his own aim.
By oblation of mallika, jati and punnaga flowers one becomes an abode of fortune; likewise by oblation of bilva fruits or their leaves.
A prince gains a kingdom; with lotuses one gains prosperity; with blue lotuses one subdues the universe, and with salt soaked in honey, a woman.
An oblation of vanjula fuel soon brings rain; an oblation of guduchi pieces smeared with milk destroys fever.
With durva one gains long life, with rice grains one becomes wealthy; with kadamba one gains control — all soaked in the three sweets.
An oblation of nandyavarta flowers gives perfection of speech; one should offer neem flowers for the prosperity one desires.
By oblation of palasha flowers a man becomes radiant. Sandal, aloe-wood, musk, camphor, saffron and gorochana,
offered and applied as a tilaka, bring control and endearment. By an oblation of nirgundi root a man is freed from fetters.
An oblation of salt with neem oil destroys enemies; with salt mixed with turmeric powder one paralyses the world.
This perfected vidya of Matangi has been told to you, best of brahmins; now I will describe another incarnation — listen.
Dipaka, Priti joined with the moon, twice, then Ranjita again, and the beloved of Fire at the end — this is the eight-syllable mantra of Dhumavati.
Its seer is Pippalada, its metre Nivrit, and its deity Dhumavati; one should form [the limbs] with the seed joined with the six long vowels and jati.
Then one should meditate on Dhumavati, who subdues enemies: pale, restless, wicked, tall, in dirty clothes,
with loose hair, thin, a widow, with sparse teeth, riding a chariot with a crow on its banner, with hanging breasts,
a winnowing basket in her hand, ... her body hair greatly grown, with crooked, squinting eyes,
always tormented by hunger and thirst, fearsome, fond of quarrels. Contemplating her thus, with 'namah svaha phat' at the end,
placing the seed above the target, and placing a corpse there, one should recite; pressing on the corpse, one should recite the mantra with the enemy's name.
Wearing a turban and jacket, the learned one, on the dark fourteenth day and night, fasting, in a cremation ground, a forest or an empty temple,
for the perfection of the mantra, restrained in speech, meditating ceaselessly on the Goddess — after a thousand recitations the enemy is seized by fever.
The fever is quelled by the five products of the cow, or by milk. Writing the first syllable of the mantra, then the enemy's name,
then the second syllable of the mantra and the enemy's name likewise — reciting the whole mantra ten thousand times brings death like a corpse's.
Burning a heron in a cremation-ground fire and taking its ashes, the knower of mantras, reciting it eight hundred times with the opponent's name, drives out the enemy.
Making a corpse-figure with cremation-ground ash and placing it on top, enclosed by the opponent's name, one should recite in the dark fortnight,
and offer incense of buffalo's milk, bringing calamity on the enemy. Thus four incarnations have been described in brief
of Durga, mother of the world; what more do you wish to ask?
Thus the vidya of Tripurasundari has been told with its seer and the rest. With Daha, Bhumi, Rasa, Kshma and Sva the Vashini seed is declared.
Prana with Rasa and Shakti is the great syllable of Kameshvari; with Shunya, Ambu, Rasa, Vahni and Sva combined, the mantra of Mohini.
Vyapta with Rasa, Kshma and Sva is declared the Vimala seed; with Jya, Nabha, Daha, Vahni and Sva combined comes the mantra of Aruna.
Of Jayini the mantra is declared, granting victory everywhere: 'ka' with Nabha and Daha, and Vyapta with Kshma and Sva.
The mantra of Sarveshvari is declared, supremely granting all success; Grasa joined with Nabha, Daha, Vahni and Sva is the mantra of Kaulini.
With these eight mantras — the Shaktis joined with their letter-groups, ending with the deity of speech — the placement is made by which one becomes of the Goddess's nature.
One should place them on the crown, forehead, ajna, throat, heart, navel, base and the two feet, from the root to the tip.
One should perform the six limbs with the seed joined with the six long vowels. One should remember the red Lalita, holding in her hands arrows, bow, noose and goad,
seated on Kameshvara's lap, established in the yantra, joyful. The central Goddess is one alone, standing in sixteen forms;
therefore the other fifteen are to be worshipped in her body. Its seer is Shiva, its metre stated, and its deities are Lalita and the rest.
The enclosures of all the Nityas I will describe in the collection of names, and the applications in detail in the chapter ahead.
Now, of the sixteen Nityas, hear, Narada, of the second, called Kameshvari, who grants all desires.
Shuchi with Sva is the first; Lalita is the second; Shunya with Agni, then Raya with Vyapta,
Prana with Rasa and Agni, a pair of Shunyas with Chara, Nabha and Gotra again, joined with Daha,
Ambu with Chara, and the heart joined with the nine Shaktis — this is the Nitya Kameshvari, the eleven-syllable granter of desire.
With the syllables of the root vidya one should perform the six limbs in order: the heart with one, the head with as many, then two by two,
the eyes with four, and the weapon is declared with one. On the eyes, ears, the two nostrils, the tongue, heart, navel and private parts,
and pervasively over all the body from head to feet, one should then place the syllables of the vidya at these places,
and perform the pervading placement with the whole, in the order described. Now I will tell of the meditation prescribed in the daily worship,
by which the Goddess, well pleased, grants one's wishes without effort: radiant as crores of rising suns, shining with a ruby crown,
adorned with necklace, neck-ornament, girdle, rings, anklets and the rest, clad in red and beautiful with jewelled ornaments,
six-armed, three-eyed, her head adorned with the digit of the moon, abiding in the pentagon, octagon, sixteen-petal pair, hexagon and square,
her face shining with a gentle smile, her glance slow with compassion, holding noose and goad, a bow of pundra sugarcane and flower arrows,
a jewelled vessel full of wine, and the gesture of boon-giving. Then, when the mantra is perfected, the practitioner should perform the applications.
Now I will tell of the third, named Bhagamalini. It begins with the first of Kameshvari, then Rasa, Chapa, Sthira, Rasa,
Dhara with Chara, then Sthira, then Rasa is remembered; Sthira and Shunya with Agni, then Rasa,
Sthira with Bhu and Gotra, Daha, Agni, Rasa, Sthira; Nabha with Maruta and joined with the letter Rasa,
then Rasa, Sthira joined with Maruta, Amba, Hamsa, Chara ... Rasa and again Sthira,
Sthira with Dhara, Hamsa with Vyapta and Chara, Rasa, Sthira, then Vyapta with Bhu, Shunya with Agni,
Rasa, Sthira, then Shunya with Agni, Marut ... Raya, Shunya with Agni, the heart, and after Hamsa,
Rasa, Sthira, Ambu, Viyat with Sva, and Prana; Daha, Agni with Rasa, then Sthira and Kshma with Daha, with Chara, Javi — the earlier vidya from the third in order.
Then a group of four letters: Rasa, then Sthira; the heart with Ambu, Daha with Kshma, with Chara, Javi and the heart;
Daha with Ambu and Maruta; in Vyoma, Agni and Rasa; Sthira joined with Maruta; Shunya, Agni, Nabha and Chara;
Hamsa with Vyapta and Maruta; Shunya, Vyapta and Ambu; Daha with Gotra and Chara; likewise Daha and Raya;
the heart with Dhara; Daha and Raya with Chara; Rasa, Sthira, then Prana with Rasa and Agni;
a pair of Shunyas with Chara, then as before; a pair of Shunyas and Gotra; Chara with Ambu joined with Vaha;
Prana, Rasa with Chara, then Gotra ...; Gotra with Daha and Marut, then the placement of Ambu;
Nabha and Bhu, with Chara; Grasa with Dhara, then Rasa with Shakti;
Grasa with Bhu, O brahmin, Rasa, Vyapta and then the heart; Daha with Ambu, then the heart; then Raya with Ambu and Maruta;
Shunya alone, and Rasa, Chara and Sthira; Viyat with Ambu, Daha with Agni and Sva, and Shuchi;
Bhumi with Rasa, Kshma and Sva; five Sthiras at intervals of one; and between them five seeds joined with Sva:
these in order — Jya with Chara, Rasa and Bhu with Nabha, Hamsa with Chara twice, then Prana with Rasa and Agni,
a pair of Shunyas with Chara, the heart, Daha with Ambu and Maruta, Vyoma with Agni, then Rasa and Sthira with Maruta,
Shunya with Agni and Nabha, with Chara; Ambu, then Viyat, then Nabha with Marut,
Shunya and Vyapta joined with 'da,' with Raya, Daha, Sva and Vahni; Hamsa with Daha, Ambu, Rasa, Chara and Sva combined;
Hamsa with Daha, Vahni and Sva is declared the last. With one hundred and thirty-seven syllables it is the Nitya Saubhagyamalini.
The limbs are formed with the letters of the mantra: the heart is declared with the first, then the head with four, the topknot with three,
and the remaining limbs with three and four syllables, six in order. [Meditate on her,] red, adorned in red, beautiful, with a smiling face,
three-eyed, with six arms, seated on a lotus, holding in her left hands a kahlara lotus, a noose and a bow of pundra sugarcane,
and in her right a lotus, a goad and a flower arrow; surrounded on all sides by praised hosts of Shaktis like herself,
and others named by the letters, full of the madness and intoxication of love. This third is declared, the enchantress of women and people.
Hear, best of brahmins, of the fourth, called Nityaklinna. Hamsa joined with Daha, Vahni and Sva is said to be first;
then there are the eight letters beginning with the third of Kameshvari; the heart joined with Ambu and Maruta — this is the eleven-syllable one.
This is the eleven-syllable one, and the limbs are formed with the letters of the vidya: the heart is declared with the first letter of the mantra,
and the remaining limbs are to be formed with two each. One should place them from the root of the thumb upward to the tip of the little finger,
and the rest on the palm; one should place the letters on the heart, eyes, ears, the two nostrils, skin, penis, anus and feet.
[Meditate on her,] red, adorned in red, wearing red garments, with red garlands and unguents, her lotus face gently smiling,
her face shining with three eyes, pearls of sweat on her forehead, radiant, the half-moon gleaming in her crown,
holding with four arms a noose, a goad, a drinking vessel and the gesture of fearlessness, seated in the middle of a lotus, languid with passion.
Meditating thus, one should worship the Nitya Nityaklinna with her own Shaktis. The holy fourth, called Nityaklinna, has been told, O sage.
[The next begins with] Vanita, Navanita, Davika, Agni, with Jaya and the rest: first Bhu with Sva, then Prana with Daha,
Rasa with Daha, Prabha with Daha, and Jya with Daha, ending with 'nityaklinna,' and the pair.
This is the nine-syllable Nitya Bherunda, granting all success. Leaving out the pranava and the two 'tha's, with the six middle syllables
one should perform the six limbs, and then the placement of the letters: on the crown, the mouth, throat, heart, navel and the two supports,
one should place the nine letters of the mantra, preceded by the placement of the alphabet. Now I will tell of the meditation on the Goddess, granting all aims:
her body like molten gold, with three eyes, gently smiling, her face radiant, adorned with divine ornaments,
decked with earrings, necklace, armlets and clusters of jewels, most beautiful with girdle, anklets, rings and other ornaments,
holding in her hands noose, goad, shield, sword, mace, thunderbolt, bow and arrows, seated in worship ...
And the Shaktis of like form, radiance and weapons — Vijaya and the others, with smiling faces — should likewise be worshipped all around.
This fifth, called Bherunda, has been described, O lord of sages; by remembering her the three kinds of poison are destroyed in a moment.
The sixth, best of brahmins, is the Nitya Vahnivasini; hear now her procedure, which grants great success to practitioners.
Here the first is the first of Bherunda, then after the first of Nityaklinna; then in Ambu and Shunya, Hamsa with Agni, and Ambu with Maruta,
Shunya with the heart and Agni, joined with Vyapta and Shuchi; Shunya and Nabha with Shakti — this is declared the nine-syllable one.
With the second seed of the vidya one should join the long vowels, ending with Maya; with these six one should perform the limbs on the hands and body.
